name: Boilerpipe (Christian Kohlschuetter, L3S Research Center Hannover), the Java library implementing 'Boilerplate Detection using Shallow Text Features' (Kohlschuetter, Fankhauser, Nejdl, WSDM 2010), which itself extends the densitometric page-segmentation work (Kohlschuetter, CIKM 2008). Ports and relatives: boilerpy3 (Python, the version benchmarked today), python-boilerpipe (JVM wrapper), BoilerNet (neural successor). The wider family of text-density heuristics includes CETD / Composite Text Density with DensitySum (Sun, Song, Liao, SIGIR 2011) and its reimplementations (bluele/cetd, FeiSun/ContentExtraction, oiwn/dom-content-extraction in Rust). Chromium's DOM Distiller is 'loosely based on Boilerpipe', so Chrome Reader Mode is downstream of this line.
kind: Research result that became a library. The WSDM 2010 paper is the primary artifact -- a feature set plus a trained classifier -- and Boilerpipe/boilerpy3/CETD are implementations of it. Treating it as 'a library' understates the point: the reusable object here is the FEATURE DEFINITION, not any codebase.
maturity: Deprecated as software, foundational as an idea. Original Boilerpipe was hosted on Google Code, mirrored to GitHub as an explicitly 'work-in-progress transmit from Google Code', and has been effectively unmaintained for over a decade; the Java version requires a JVM toolchain nobody in this space runs. boilerpy3 is the maintained Python reimplementation and is what modern benchmarks actually measure. The IDEAS are current -- text density and link density are still the substrate under jusText, DOM Distiller, and much of the density-based literature -- but no shipping system should take a dependency on the original code.
license: Boilerpipe: Apache-2.0 [uncertain] -- the GitHub mirror carries a LICENSE file whose type I could not confirm from the repository page, though Apache-2.0 is what the Google Code original declared and what downstream packaging asserts. boilerpy3: Apache-2.0. CETD reimplementations vary (MIT and Apache-2.0 among them). The FEATURE DEFINITIONS -- text density, link density, block segmentation -- are published algorithms in a peer-reviewed paper and are not encumbered; reimplementing them from the paper avoids the license question entirely and is the sane path.
keeps_and_discards: Boilerpipe segments the page into ATOMIC TEXT BLOCKS by splitting at block-level tags (the inline/block distinction from HTML itself, nothing else), then classifies each block as content or boilerplate from shallow quantitative features, then concatenates the content blocks. The features are the whole idea: number of words in the block, average word length, average sentence length, TEXT DENSITY (words per line at a fixed notional wrap width, typically 80 characters -- a proxy for how prose-like a block is), LINK DENSITY (fraction of the block's words sitting inside anchors), relative position in the document, capitalized-word ratio, and -- critically -- the same features for the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING and FOLLOWING blocks. What survives is prose; what is dropped is navigation (high link density, low word count), footers, copyright lines, ad captions and menu chains. The shipped extractor variants apply different post-filters: DefaultExtractor (general), ArticleExtractor (news-tuned, with title handling), ArticleSentencesExtractor, LargestContentExtractor, KeepEverythingExtractor, KeepEverythingWithMinKWordsExtractor, NumWordsRulesExtractor, CanolaExtractor. NOTE what is absent from every feature in the list: no class names, no ids, no tag semantics beyond block-vs-inline, no URL patterns, no region vocabulary. That absence is the reason this item matters.
structure_preserved: Almost nothing in classic Boilerpipe, and this is its worst property. Output is a flat sequence of content blocks -- text with block boundaries -- so headings are not distinguished from paragraphs, list structure is gone, tables are destroyed (a table becomes a stream of low-word-count blocks that the classifier tends to discard wholesale), nesting is gone, and document order is the only structural fact retained. Blocks carry a label and their text, nothing else. CETD is the significant improvement here and is the reason it is worth naming separately: it computes density over DOM NODES rather than over a flattened block sequence, explicitly 'to preserve the original structure', and its DensitySum technique (replacing data smoothing) is designed to extract content INTACT rather than as a filtered stream. So the family spans from Boilerpipe's total structural loss to CETD's node-level preservation, using the same underlying quantity. Shadow boundaries are outside all of it -- these are 2010-2011 algorithms over serialized HTML, and open shadow roots are simply absent with no unreachable marker.
interactive_elements: Discarded, and discarded by the feature design rather than by an explicit rule -- which is a subtler and more interesting failure than an explicit strip list. Controls carry few words and, when wrapped in anchors, high link density, so they land on the boilerplate side of the classifier automatically. Nothing in the pipeline names a form, a button or an input; they are eliminated as a statistical consequence of being short and link-dense. The output is text with no notion of a control, no element type, no href, and no label-to-input association. There is no toggle to keep them (contrast Resiliparse's form_fields), because the representation has no slot to put them in.
interactive_state_fidelity: Zero, with no partial credit available. disabled, checked, selected, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-current and role are not read as features, not carried through blocks, and not representable in the output, which is untyped text. aria-* plays no role at all -- not even the negative role it plays in Readability and Resiliparse, since Boilerpipe has no visibility pass to speak of. Token cost of state: zero. Affordance count: zero. Boilerpipe is the purest expression in this batch of the assumption that a web page is a noisy container for an article, and it is worth keeping as the reference point for how completely that assumption erases the acting surface. Note the asymmetry with its own strength: the feature set is admirably agnostic about STRUCTURE while being totally committed about PURPOSE.
layout_awareness: None geometric, and this is a deliberate and defended design position rather than an omission. Text density is a proxy FOR layout -- 'words per line at a notional 80-character wrap' is an estimate of how a block would render without rendering it -- and the paper's framing (features with 'a strong correspondence to stochastic text models introduced in the field of Quantitative Linguistics') argues that the quantitative-linguistic signal is what carries the information, not the pixels. Modern commentary on boilerpy3 makes the same point from the other side: it extracts content 'without considering page layout'. This is the most important structural fact about the item for this project: text density is a LAYOUT-FREE PROXY FOR A LAYOUT PROPERTY, computed from text alone, and it is the existence proof that some of what geometry buys can be bought without geometry.
javascript_required: No, and it cannot use it. Static HTML in, text out; no browser, no rendering, no script execution, no subresource fetching, hence no telemetry fired at read time. SPAs yield the shell. In this project's architecture the browser has already executed the page, so the no-JS property buys no privacy and the SPA blindness is pure cost -- but unlike the heavier extractors, the ALGORITHM has no dependency on serialized-HTML input at all: text density and link density are computable directly over a live composed DOM's text nodes. Nothing in the mathematics requires the static-HTML setting; only the implementations assume it.
evaluation_method: The WSDM 2010 paper frames extraction as per-block BINARY CLASSIFICATION -- each atomic text block is labelled content or boilerplate by human assessors, and the model is scored as a classifier with a decision tree (Weka's C4.8/J48) trained on the shallow features, with a linear SVM as a comparison. This is a materially different and in some respects better methodology than everything else in this batch: the unit of judgement is a block rather than a whole-page span, so the oracle is asked many small, concrete questions instead of one large, contestable one, and the resulting metric is a genuine classification precision/recall rather than a bag-of-words overlap. The paper additionally validates EXTRINSICALLY on the BLOGS06 retrieval benchmark, showing that removing boilerplate improves retrieval precision -- a downstream-task oracle in the same spirit as DCLM's, and unusual for 2010. CETD evaluates against CleanEval plus randomly selected pages from well-known websites. Modern re-measurement of boilerpy3 comes from WCXB (word-bag F1) and the Webis SIGIR 2023 reproducibility study (ROUGE-LSum and Levenshtein).
corpus_size_and_origins: L3S-GN1, released with Boilerpipe: 621 news pages sampled from Google News, English, collected around January 2010 (the distribution directory is timestamped 20100130). Origin count is not prominently reported and I could not verify it, nor could I verify the number of assessors or any inter-annotator agreement statistic -- both are [uncertain], and the absence of a published kappa on a per-block annotation task is a real gap given that block-level boilerplate judgements are exactly where annotators would be expected to disagree. BLOGS06 is a TREC blog collection, large but from 2006 and blog-only. CETD used CleanEval (684 English plus 653 Chinese pages, downloaded 2006, published 2007) plus an unspecified hand-picked set. Every corpus in this item is between 15 and 20 years old, news-or-blog-dominated, and predates responsive layout, SPAs, consent banners and shadow DOM entirely. The generation gap is the largest in this batch, and it matters more than usual because the density thresholds were TUNED to the typographic conventions of that era's pages.
reported_precision_recall: The paper's headline: a very small feature set suffices, with the two-feature classifier over link density and number of words (using the current and previous block) reaching roughly F1 0.95 on L3S-GN1 -- a figure that should be read as 'per-block classification accuracy on 2010 English news', not as extraction quality on the modern web. [uncertain] on the exact decimal, since I could not extract the results table from the paper PDF. Modern re-measurement on modern pages is far lower and is the number that should be quoted: WCXB word-bag F1 places BoilerPy3 at 0.687 on 1,497 development pages -- seventh of eight systems, above only Readability's 0.674 and below Trafilatura's 0.791, Resiliparse's 0.797 and rs-trafilatura's 0.859. The 0.95-to-0.687 gap between the 2010 self-reported figure and the 2026 third-party figure is the single most useful number pair in this item: it is a direct measurement of how far a density heuristic tuned on 2010 news degrades on the 2026 web, and it is a warning that any threshold tuned to a corpus decays with the corpus.
independent_oracle: Partially yes, and better than most here. The BLOGS06 retrieval evaluation is a genuine independent oracle: it does not ask 'did you match the human's span', it asks 'did retrieval precision improve', which shares no assumption with the extractor and cannot be gamed by agreeing with an annotator. That is the same class of oracle DCLM later used for Resiliparse, arriving fifteen years earlier and largely uncredited. The primary oracle (per-block human labels) is not independent -- it encodes the content/boilerplate dichotomy the classifier learns -- but its GRANULARITY is a real methodological advance: many small judgements are more auditable and more disagreement-tolerant than one whole-page span, and disagreement shows up as classifier noise rather than as an unfalsifiable difference of opinion about where the article begins. WCXB's word-bag oracle, applied to boilerpy3 today, shares assumptions with the tool in the usual way.
evidence_independence: The 0.95-class figure is AUTHOR-RUN: Kohlschuetter, Fankhauser and Nejdl evaluating their own classifier on a dataset (L3S-GN1) they built and released, at their own institution (L3S). It should be read as the ceiling an interested party could produce on a corpus of their own choosing. The BLOGS06 extrinsic result is also author-run but on a pre-existing TREC collection they did not build, which raises its credibility considerably. The 0.687 WCXB figure is THIRD-PARTY, produced by an author (Foley) whose own tool tops that leaderboard -- so it is a competitor's measurement, but a competitor with no particular reason to single out a fifteen-year-old library, and boilerpy3's low placement is unsurprising rather than suspicious. The Webis SIGIR 2023 numbers are likewise competitor-run (Resiliparse's authors). Net: unlike Trafilatura versus rs-trafilatura, there is no contradiction to resolve here -- author-run and competitor-run figures agree about the shape (excellent on 2010 news, mediocre on the 2026 web), and the disagreement is entirely explained by corpus era.
page_archetype_coverage: Single archetype, and narrower than Readability's. L3S-GN1 is news; BLOGS06 is blogs; the ArticleExtractor variant is explicitly news-tuned. The feature set encodes an implicit archetype prior that is not about markup but about TYPOGRAPHY: it assumes the valuable content is the part with long, prose-like, low-link-density runs of text. That assumption is false for exactly the archetypes this project cares about -- a search-results listing is entirely high-link-density blocks and will be classified as boilerplate in its entirety; a product page is short attribute-value fragments and will be discarded as low-word-count; a forum is many short blocks each below the word-count threshold; a documentation page is code and tables that carry no sentence structure. WCXB does not publish a per-type breakdown for BoilerPy3 that I could retrieve, so the archetype spread is [uncertain] numerically, but it is predictable structurally and the prediction is severe: the failure is not degradation, it is total rejection of link-dense and fragment-dense pages. For a sensor whose targets include listings and result pages, a density heuristic is close to worst-case.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Explicitly and unusually language-sensitive, and the paper is candid that this is the point rather than a bug -- the features are argued to correspond to stochastic text models from quantitative linguistics, i.e. to statistical regularities of a LANGUAGE. Average word length, average sentence length and words-per-line are all language-dependent quantities, and thresholds tuned on English or German do not transfer: German's longer compounds shift average word length, and CJK breaks the entire framework because word counts require segmentation that the algorithm does not perform and because words-per-line at an 80-character wrap means something completely different when a character carries a morpheme. CETD's evaluation on CleanEval's Chinese half is the one piece of cross-script evidence in the family and it is 2006-era. No RTL handling, no bidi isolation on output, and no whitespace-free segmentation support. The honest reading: text density is a POWERFUL and STRUCTURE-agnostic feature that is NOT SCRIPT-INVARIANT, and any adoption must either recalibrate per script or replace word counts with a script-neutral unit (graphemes, or bytes of normalized text) and re-derive the thresholds.
leaks_outward: Nothing. Pure computation over text already in hand: no network access, no telemetry, no phone-home, no model download (the decision tree is tiny and embedded), no fetcher shipped with the extraction path. It is the lowest-disclosure item in the batch alongside Resiliparse, and unlike Trafilatura it has no crawler mode to accidentally invoke. Whatever performs the fetch owns the entire disclosure question.
mechanism_detectability: Zero, and unimprovable-upon. It does not run in the page, patches no DOM API, never touches attachShadow, opens no CDP session, installs no extension, and creates no timing side channel because it is not present while the page is live. It is absent by construction. More usefully for this project: because the features are computable over a live composed DOM's text nodes with no API beyond reading text content, a text-density peripheral could be computed INSIDE a browser session using only the same reads the fold already performs -- adding no new detectable surface whatsoever. That is a rare property. Most signals worth having cost an observable access pattern; text density costs nothing the sensor is not already doing.
countermeasures: None needed and none offered. The countermeasures that exist run against it and are trivial: any site wanting to defeat a density extractor pads its boilerplate with prose or fragments its article into short blocks, and client-side rendering defeats it outright. There is no hardening dimension because there is nothing to detect. The one operational safeguard the family lacks entirely is a resource bound -- unlike Resiliparse's Process Guards, a pathological document has no guard rail, though the algorithm's linear cost makes this a minor concern.
measured_fidelity_cost: Measured in an unusual and partly useful way, and unmeasured in the way this project needs. The BLOGS06 result is a genuine cost/benefit measurement against a real control -- retrieval precision with boilerplate versus without -- which is more than most items here have, but it measures downstream UTILITY, not fidelity, and it cannot detect content that was wrongly discarded so long as retrieval still improved. Nothing measures loss against the full capture. Affordance retention is structurally zero. What CAN be quoted as a fidelity cost is the era-decay figure derived above: the same algorithmic family scoring ~0.95 on its own 2010 news corpus and 0.687 on a 2026 mixed corpus implies roughly a 27-point absolute drop attributable to corpus drift, and that number is the most transferable warning in this item -- it is what happens to any tuned threshold left in place while the web moves, and it bears directly on this project's frozen-versus-live corpus problem.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded, not representable, and additionally distorted. There is no consent, paywall, login or CAPTCHA field. Worse than neutral: consent-banner copy is typically a medium-length, low-link-density prose block -- structurally indistinguishable from an article paragraph under this feature set -- so a density extractor will confidently classify consent text as CONTENT. Paywall teasers likewise present as clean prose and extract as complete articles. With roughly two-thirds of top sites presenting a consent interface, a Boilerpipe-built corpus does not merely mix gated and ungated captures, it actively enriches for consent text, which then appears in the corpus as ordinary prose with no marker. This is the specific way density heuristics poison a modern corpus and it is not discussed in the literature.
determinism: Fully deterministic within a pinned version and pinned model: a fixed decision tree evaluated on features computed by pure arithmetic over text, with no randomness, no clock, no network, no cross-call state, and no learned component that is refit at runtime. Same input, same output, and idempotent across repeated calls in one process. Of everything in this batch, this is the cleanest determinism story -- there is not even Trafilatura's dedup-cache caveat or Resiliparse's process-guard caveat. The one boundary case is float comparison at a threshold: a block whose density sits exactly on a split point can flip with a change in floating-point evaluation order across platforms or JIT states, which is a real if rare portability concern for a decision tree with continuous features.
determinism_across_versions: Drifts only through the parser and the variant choice, which is a narrow surface. The classifier is frozen -- the trained tree from 2010 is what ships -- so the model itself does not move, which is unusual and good. What does move: the HTML parser underneath (Java's parser, or boilerpy3's, changing whitespace normalisation, entity handling and implied-element insertion, which changes block segmentation and therefore every feature value), and the choice of extractor variant, which is a caller decision that silently changes output character. The frozen model is a double-edged property: it guarantees version stability and it guarantees the tool never adapts, which is exactly how the 0.95-to-0.687 decay happened. Stability across versions and relevance across years are in direct tension here, and Boilerpipe is the clean demonstration.
reproducibility: Good in principle and awkward in practice. L3S-GN1 was released with the system, so the primary result is re-runnable if the dataset is still retrievable and the JVM toolchain can be resurrected; BLOGS06 is a TREC collection with controlled distribution. boilerpy3 plus WCXB's CC-BY-4.0 release is fully re-runnable today and is the practical path. The deeper reproducibility lesson is about the CORPUS rather than the code: the algorithm reproduces its 2010 numbers on 2010 pages perfectly and reproduces nothing on 2026 pages, which is exactly the failure mode a frozen evaluation corpus produces. This is the clearest available argument that a frozen corpus is necessary but not sufficient -- it must be frozen AND periodically re-sampled, with both generations kept, or the tool silently drifts out from under its evidence.
failure_modes: (1) Wholesale rejection of link-dense pages: a listing or search-results page is all high-link-density blocks and returns empty or near-empty. This is the dominant failure on this project's target archetypes and it is total rather than gradual. (2) Fragment rejection: product attributes, table cells, forum posts and captions fall below word-count thresholds and are discarded en masse. (3) Consent and paywall text promoted to content, as described above. (4) Structural annihilation: even on a successful extraction, headings, lists and tables are flattened into an untyped block stream, so 'success' still destroys structure -- CETD is the fix and is not what anyone benchmarks. (5) Boundary bleed: because features include the previous and next block, a single anomalous block can flip its neighbours, producing runs of misclassification rather than isolated errors. (6) Threshold decay: unchanged thresholds against a changed web, which is not an event but a slow degradation nobody observes. (7) SPA shell.
failure_visibility: Mixed, with one honest signal available and unexploited. Empty output on a link-dense page is loud and trivially detectable by a length check, and because the dominant failure on modern non-article pages is TOTAL rejection rather than subtle mis-selection, the failure is more visible than Readability's. But the classifier produces a per-block DECISION and, in a decision tree, an implicit margin -- and neither Boilerpipe nor boilerpy3 surfaces per-block confidence, block counts, or the content/boilerplate ratio, all of which are free and would turn the remaining silent failures into observable ones. That omission is worth naming precisely because it is so cheap to fix: a per-block classifier that reports its label distribution is self-describing almost for free, and none of these implementations do it. Threshold decay (failure 6) is invisible by construction and is the one that actually matters over time.
scale_limits: The cheapest in the batch. A single pass to segment blocks, a constant-time feature computation per block, and a shallow decision-tree evaluation per block -- linear in text length with a tiny constant, no multi-pass cascade, no global optimisation, no model inference beyond a handful of comparisons. It is streaming-compatible in principle since blocks arrive in order and the classifier needs only the previous and next block, which means it could run over a document as it parses rather than after -- a property no other extractor in this batch has and which nobody appears to have exploited. Memory is bounded by the block sequence, not the DOM. This is the algorithm you would pick if cost were the only criterion.
delta_cost_model: THE STANDOUT FINDING OF THIS ITEM, and the reason it earns a place in this batch despite being obsolete software. Boilerpipe is the ONLY classic extractor here whose classification decision is LOCAL. Text density, link density, word count, average word length and average sentence length are all computed from a single block's own text; the only non-local dependency is the immediately preceding and following block. Therefore a change to one block's text invalidates AT MOST THREE blocks' classifications -- itself and its two neighbours -- and the recomputation cost is proportional to the changed text, not to the page. That is a genuine, provable O(delta) recomputation model, and it stands in exact contrast to Readability's global top-candidate scoring (where a one-character change can flip the winning subtree) and to rs-trafilatura's whole-page feature vector. The caveats are precise and must be stated: (a) the BLOCK SEGMENTATION must itself be maintained incrementally, which is tractable since it is driven by block-level tag boundaries, but a structural mutation that merges or splits blocks propagates further than a text edit; (b) the shipped ArticleExtractor variants add post-filters that use document-level statistics (largest-block selection, title expansion), and those reintroduce global dependence -- so the delta property belongs to the CORE DENSITOMETRIC CLASSIFIER, not to the packaged extractors; (c) changes outside the model remain outside it entirely: shadow mutations, CSS-driven change, canvas, and declarative shadow DOM in the initial parse are all invisible, so an O(delta) claim built on this must be paired with a separate accounting for those classes rather than inheriting silence about them.
reanchoring_stability: No identity is carried in the output, but the internal representation is closer to supporting it than anything else here. Blocks are ordinal and positional -- block N of the sequence -- which is a weak identity that survives text edits within a block but breaks on any insertion or deletion that shifts the sequence, so as a re-anchoring key it is unusable. CETD's node-level formulation is materially better because density is computed PER DOM NODE, so the density value is naturally keyed by node address rather than by sequence position, and that is directly compatible with an xpath-keyed store: a per-node scalar attached to an addressable node is exactly the shape of a peripheral. No implementation publishes a re-anchor rate and none carries content hashes or offsets. The adoptable form is CETD's, not Boilerpipe's: compute the density scalar per addressed node, store it beside the node, and re-anchoring becomes the trie's problem rather than the extractor's.
adversarial_exposure: Substantially exposed, with a distinctive and under-appreciated twist. Boilerpipe has essentially NO visibility pass -- weaker even than Readability's inline-style check -- so attribute-level concealment (display:none in a style attribute, the hidden attribute, aria-hidden) passes straight through in the base algorithm, alongside all stylesheet-driven, off-screen, zero-size and colour-matched concealment. It is the most concealment-exposed item in the batch. The twist is that its FEATURE SET is unusually attacker-legible: an adversary who wants text kept need only make it prose-like and link-free, which is precisely what a well-written injected instruction paragraph already is. A density classifier does not merely fail to filter injected prose -- it PREFERS it, because injected instructions are typically clean, unlinked, medium-length sentences, which is the exact profile of the highest-scoring content block. That inverts the deletion-volume accident that protects Readability. Set against this project's position: a layout-blind fold is exposed, and a layout-blind fold that additionally RANKS by prose-likeness would be actively selecting for injection payloads. If text density is adopted as a peripheral, it must not be allowed to drive inclusion.
provenance_carrying: None, at any granularity, in any implementation. No url, no xpath, no offsets, no capture time, no shadow depth, no gate state, no block-to-source mapping in the output. The block sequence discards its own addresses. CETD again does better structurally by virtue of being node-based -- a density value computed at a DOM node is implicitly addressed by that node even though no implementation persists the address. The generalisable point for this project: text density is a PER-NODE SCALAR, which is exactly the shape that fits a peripheral keyed by address, and the reason no implementation carries provenance is that all of them immediately flatten the node tree into a text stream. Do not flatten, and the provenance problem does not arise.
roundtrip_safety: Not a fixed point, and it fails in an especially clean way that makes it a good demonstration. Feeding Boilerpipe's output back into Boilerpipe yields a much smaller result or nothing, because the extracted text has been stripped of the anchors and short blocks that gave the retained blocks their contrast -- link density is a RELATIVE signal and the transform destroys the comparison set. That is a sharper version of the general problem: any extractor whose features are contrastive cannot be idempotent, because extraction removes the contrast. This is worth stating as a design rule rather than as a fact about one tool: a fold that must be a round-trip fixed point cannot rank by contrast against material it removes. There is no escaping policy at all -- output is raw text with block boundaries as newlines, so source text containing the boundary convention is indistinguishable from a boundary, and no implementation claims sanitization of any kind.
token_budget_and_ordering: No budget, no truncation policy, and document order in the output -- but the family supplies the single most useful ORDERING PRIMITIVE in this batch, which is the reason to care about it here. Text density is a per-block (or per-node, in CETD) continuous score of prose-likeness, computed with no page-structure prior, no region names, no geometry, and no model. That is a legitimate ranking signal for deciding what goes early in a context window and what gets truncated first, and it is computable incrementally. Given that past 50% context fill position bias becomes recency-dominant, having ANY principled, cheap, structure-agnostic scalar to order by is worth more than a marginal improvement in extraction quality. The critical constraint from the adversarial analysis above: density may inform ORDER and must not inform INCLUSION, because ranking by prose-likeness is ranking by exactly the profile an injected instruction has. Order by it, cap the budget elsewhere, and never let it delete.
representation_cost: Extreme compression -- typically well under 10% of source token count on an article and effectively 0% on link-dense pages, since those return empty. Per token saved, it discards more than any other item here: all structure (not merely the ancestor chain, but headings, lists and tables), all affordances, all state, all addressability, all provenance. It is the cheapest and the lossiest point on the curve, which makes it useful as the lower bound of the compression/fidelity tradeoff. CETD costs more tokens and returns structure, and the delta between them is a reasonable estimate of what preserving nesting costs in this family: [uncertain] numerically, since no one has published the comparison in token terms.
what_could_be_adopted: This is the highest-yield item in the batch for mechanism transfer, precisely because it is obsolete as software and durable as mathematics. (1) TEXT DENSITY AS A PER-NODE PERIPHERAL SCALAR, in CETD's node-keyed formulation rather than Boilerpipe's flattened-block one. It is structure-agnostic in the strict sense the project means -- it reads no class, no id, no role, no URL, and names no region; it is a layout-free proxy for a layout property, so it recovers part of what no_layout_in_the_fold gives up without reading geometry; it is computable from text alone, so it adds no detectable access pattern beyond what the fold already does; and it attaches naturally to an xpath-addressed node. (2) LINK DENSITY, same properties, with the same caveat. (3) THE LOCALITY PROPERTY as a design constraint to imitate: features that depend only on a node and its immediate neighbours give a provable O(delta) recomputation bound, and Boilerpipe is the existence proof that useful content signals can be built that way. Adopt the LOCALITY DISCIPLINE, not the classifier. (4) BLOCK SEGMENTATION FROM THE INLINE/BLOCK TAG DISTINCTION ALONE -- a page partition that uses only HTML's own structural vocabulary and no semantics, which is very close to the project's 'tag plus interactivity' position and is a ready-made, well-tested segmentation rule. (5) THE EXTRINSIC EVALUATION PATTERN: BLOGS06's downstream-retrieval oracle, fifteen years before DCLM did the same thing, is the template for evaluating a fold by whether it improves a downstream task rather than by whether it matches a human's span. What must NOT be adopted: the trained content/boilerplate classifier, the word-count and sentence-length thresholds (language-specific and era-decayed), and any use of density to decide INCLUSION.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: SPLIT, and the split is the most favourable in this batch. The FEATURES are ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- text density, link density, word count and block segmentation read no class, no id, no role, no ARIA, no URL pattern, and encode no region vocabulary; they are quantitative functions of text and of the inline/block tag distinction, which is exactly 'tag plus interactivity' territory. The CLASSIFIER is REJECTED: labelling a block 'boilerplate' is naming a region's role, and the trained tree encodes a 2010 news-page prior. Take the features, refuse the label. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and better than merely compliant -- text density is explicitly a layout-free substitute for a layout signal, which is the constraint's ideal case rather than a grudging accommodation. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the core densitometric classifier, and the only such verdict in this batch. Per-block features with at-most-neighbour dependence give a change-proportional recomputation bound; the packaged ArticleExtractor post-filters are REJECTED because they reintroduce document-level statistics; and shadow, CSS-driven, canvas and declarative-shadow-DOM changes remain outside the model and must be accounted for separately rather than inherited as silence. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Pure arithmetic, no model to stub beyond a frozen tree that should not be adopted anyway, no network, no learned component in the measured path, and the features are computable against a real live DOM without any simulation layer. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the features -- they compute over whatever text nodes they are given, including a composed shadow DOM's, with no need to patch attachShadow or reach into closed roots; the historical IMPLEMENTATIONS are NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY, since they consume serialized HTML, miss shadow content entirely and emit no unreachable marker. OVERALL VERDICT: the software is REJECTED (obsolete, structurally destructive, era-decayed, 0.687 on the modern web); the FEATURE SET is ADOPTABLE AS-IS as an ordering peripheral, subject to the hard rule that density informs ORDER and never INCLUSION, and to script-neutral recalibration of any thresholds.
governance_signal_handling: None, and cleanly none -- no fetcher exists in any implementation, so there is no robots.txt path, no Content Signals parsing, no ai.txt, no IETF AIPREF vocabulary, no Web Bot Auth signature or Signature Agent Card, and no HTTP 402 handling. The entire governance obligation belongs to whatever produced the HTML. Adopting the features contributes nothing either way to a governance story, which is the correct separation: a scalar computed over text the user's own browser already rendered raises no access-permission question at all, and that is a point worth making explicitly when the features are adopted, since it distinguishes computing a signal over already-loaded content from crawling.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The algorithms retain nothing; the caller's persisted artifact is the regulated act under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026. What they hand you to persist is prose stripped of everything that would help a lawful-basis analysis: no url, no capture time, no gate state, no author attribution (which cuts both ways -- less identifying metadata retained, but also no ability to distinguish editorial copy from user-generated content). Because the classifier keeps prose-like blocks, forum posts and comments that clear the word-count threshold are retained as content indistinguishable from editorial text, with no toggle to exclude them -- worse than Trafilatura's explicit include_comments switch and worse than Readability's accidental exclusion. Combined with the consent-text enrichment noted above, a density-built store contains an unmarked mixture of editorial copy, user-generated content and consent-banner text with no field to separate them. If only the SCALARS are adopted rather than the extraction, none of this applies: a per-node density number is not personal data and carries no PII posture at all, which is a further argument for taking the feature and leaving the tool.
